# Affine frustum record hulls and an all-dimensional upper-dual reduction

This note independently checks the cone/frustum reduction, falsifies one overly strong record-hull simplification, and proves a substantial branch of the proposed all-dimensional upper dual. It does not establish the remaining scalar inequality or OC.

Dependencies: `candidate 6146c77d1d7c5e08`, `candidate 0ab50bc17861492a`. The planar completion is in `candidate d28e829ed5b07592`.

## 1. Independent audit of the physical reduction

Use a in (0,1) for the source parameter 1/(H+1), not for the top radius. For d>=2 the full-cone layer records are e_s=C_s/C_0, k_s=1-v_s, and m_s=partial_a e_s. The normalized physical section moment is M_s/C_0=-(1-a)m_s/d. Thus centering is exactly E m_s=0.

For 0<s<=1,

    e_s=[(1-as)^(1-d)-(1+as)^(1-d)]/[2sa(d-1)],
    k_s=0.

For s>=1,

    e_s=[(1-a)^(1-d)-(1+as)^(1-d)]/[2sa(d-1)],
    k_s=(s-1)/(2s).

At zero, (e,m,k)=(1,0,0). These follow by integrating the uniform base law on [-s,s] over b<=1. Differentiating gives the stated moment because d/da (1-ab)^(-d)=d b(1-ab)^(-d-1).

The ray computation gives P/V_0=p_0 e+k, where p_0=(1-a)^d. For a frustum with bounded-slope threshold T>=1, every s<=T loses the whole removed top mass t V_0, with

    t=[(1-a)/(1+aT)]^d.

Both C and M are unchanged. For s>=T the full section covers the axial interval, so its record is (T/s) times the record at T plus (1-T/s) times (V/2,0,0). This preserves P,C,M simultaneously and makes the finite part of every centered law separately centered. The exceptional rays at the threshold have zero uniform-layer probability, including the cutoff layer s=T. The cases T<=1 have only the zero finite centered layer, by pairing positive and negative b in the truncated moment integral; infinity has zero coarea and moment.

The cone energy bounds 2v-1<=e<=(2v-1)/v have also been checked directly: the lower bound uses the symmetric mass on [-1,1], and the upper proof's exponent comparison and the concavity I_k''(x)=-k/(x+k)^3 have their stated signs. Atoms at zero and unbounded mixtures of finite uniform layers cause no differentiation problem on compact a-intervals, since the negative tail of every differentiated integrand is bounded.

Consequently the common-c correction question is exactly the stated simultaneous ratio problem, not a replacement of a fiber sum by an integral:

    sup_centered [v-(1-gamma)(1-t)]/e
      <= inf_centered [v-gamma(1-t)]/e.

## 2. The full centered record section is not a segment

Take d=2, a=1/4, T=3. On s>=1,

    e_s=(s+1)/[2s(1-a)(1+as)],
    m_s=e_s[1/(1-a)-s/(1+as)].

The only finite individually centered slopes are s=0 and s=2. Their (e,v) records are (1,1) and (2/3,3/4).

At slopes 1 and 3 the records are respectively

    (e,m,v)=(16/15,128/225,1),
    (e,m,v)=(32/63,-256/1323,2/3).

The probability law

    mu=(50/197)delta_1+(147/197)delta_3

has zero moment and (e,v)=(128/197,148/197). At this v, the segment joining the two individually centered records has e=395/591, whereas this law has e=384/591. Thus equality of the full centered record section with that segment is false. In particular, an arbitrary centered law cannot retain all records after replacement by horizontal plus one other slope: that other slope would itself have to be centered.

This does not contradict a directional extremum theorem for the two particular ratio objectives.

## 3. Exact support-size reduction which does hold

On a fixed compact interval [0,T], e_s is continuous and strictly positive, and m_s,k_s are continuous. The set of probability laws with E m=0 is weakly compact. Every linear-fractional functional E f/E e attains its maximum and minimum. At an attained ratio R, extremizing the linear functional E(f-Re) gives the same value. Its extreme feasible laws have support of size at most two: three disjoint positive-mass support neighborhoods admit a nonzero signed perturbation preserving total mass and moment, contrary to extremality. The usual limiting version with compact supports follows by the same finite-partition perturbation or the elementary moment-set extreme-point theorem; no differentiability of an optimizer is required.

An explicit decomposition avoids even that theorem. For any centered mu, let mu_+,mu_- be its restrictions to m>0,m<0 and M=integral m dmu_+=integral(-m)dmu_-. If M>0, set

    nu_+=(m/M)mu_+,  nu_-=(-m/M)mu_-.

For a positive-moment x and negative-moment y, let pi_xy be the centered two-point probability assigning weight -m_y/(m_x-m_y) to x. Integrating pi_xy against

    M[1/m_x+1/(-m_y)] dnu_+(x)dnu_-(y)

recovers mu_++mu_-. The total mixing mass is mu_+([0,T])+mu_-([0,T]). The restriction to m=0 is left unchanged. Tonelli applies to these nonnegative kernels. Therefore every centered record is a convex mixture of opposite-sign centered pairs and individually centered records. Every ratio is correspondingly a positive e-weighted average of pair/singleton ratios.

## 4. There is one nonzero centered slope

For s>=1 write q=1+as and

    F(q)=(dq-d+1)q^(-d),
    c=(1-da)(1-a)^(-d).

Direct differentiation gives

    m_s=[F(q)-c]/[2a(d-1)(q-1)].                 (1)

Here F'(q)=-d(d-1)(q-1)q^(-d-1)<0 for q>1. For 0<s<=1 the moment m_s is positive by symmetric pairing. If a>=1/d, c<=0 and every finite positive slope has positive m. Otherwise c>0, and there is a unique R>1+a with F(R)=c; its slope is s_*=(R-1)/a. Moments are positive below s_* and negative above it. Thus when T<s_* only the horizontal finite law is centered.

In the nontrivial case define

    e_*=e_(s_*), v_*=1-k_(s_*), p=(1-a)^d,
    t_*=[(1-a)/R]^d,
    kappa=(v_*+t)/(1+e_*), B=1+t-kappa.

The candidate common correction is (V_0/C_0)(p-kappa). Its proposed upper bound is

    E[kappa e_s+k_s] <= B.                       (2)

At s=s_* equality holds. The corresponding lower bound would be E[kappa e+k]>=kappa. The candidate paid fraction is (kappa-t)/(1-t).

The range 0<=t<=t_* means kappa lies between kappa_0=v_*/(1+e_*) and kappa_1=(v_*+t_*)/(1+e_*). The cone energy bounds give e_*<=v_* and kappa_0>=4/9. Hence the candidate paid fraction is at least 4/9. The independent proof in `candidate ff46898305c5fc7e` supplies its upper bound 1/2 and the identities

    2p<=1+t_*,  2v_*-1=2p e_*-t_*.              (C)

That proof has been independently checked: the section density r^(d-2) has mean zero, a decreasing density has median at most its mean by convexity of its quantile, and the decreasing tilt r decreases its right-hand mass. The full-section identity P=V/2+M then supplies the second equality in (C). Below, B>=kappa is exactly the paid-fraction upper bound. We also have the distinct bound B>=1/2 throughout the actual kappa interval: B=kappa e_*+1-v_* increases with kappa, and B(kappa_0)=1-kappa_0>=1/2, since e_*>=2v_*-1 gives kappa_0<=1/2.

## 5. The exact tangent dual and its Bregman form

Set

    lambda=a^2 R^(d+1)[kappa/p-1]/[d(R-1)^2],
    beta=lambda/a.

Use m=e_a, so the residual to prove is

    H(s)=B-kappa e_s-k_s+lambda m_s.             (3)

It vanishes with its first s-derivative at s_*. This follows either directly or from

    d_q(kappa e+k)|_R=a[1-kappa/p]/[2(R-1)^2],
    d_q m|_R=-d R^(-d-1)/(2a).

For s>=1 define

    Psi(q)=[(kappa+d beta)q-(d-1)beta]q^(-d).

Then exact cancellation of the affine terms gives

    2(q-1)H(s)
      =[Psi(q)-Psi(R)-Psi'(R)(q-R)]/(d-1).       (4)

In particular

    Psi''(q)=d(d-1)q^(-d-2)
                 [(kappa+d beta)q-(d+1)beta].   (5)

Thus its curvature numerator is linear, in every dimension.

## 6. A monotone ratio of power remainders

For r>0 let D_r(x)=x^(-r)-1+r(x-1), continuously interpreted at x=1 after taking ratios. Then D_(r+1)(x)/D_r(x) is strictly decreasing on x>0, with value (r+2)/r at 1 and limit (r+1)/r at infinity.

Proof. Taylor's integral formula writes the ratio as (r+2)/r times the mean of 1/t under the density proportional to (x-t)t^(-r-2) on [1,x] for x>1, or (t-x)t^(-r-2) on [x,1] for x<1. As x increases, either family shifts strictly to the right in monotone likelihood ratio order: on the common support the quotient of the later density by the earlier one is increasing in t, and new or removed support lies on the corresponding right or left side. The expectation of the strictly decreasing function 1/t therefore decreases. This likelihood-ratio implication follows directly by writing the difference of the two expectations as a double integral of [1/t-1/u] times the cross-density difference. Taylor expansion supplies the value at 1 and the leading linear terms supply the infinity limit.

The remainder in (4), with x=q/R, equals

    R^(1-d) D_(d-1)(x)
      [kappa+d beta-(d-1)beta/R
                         D_d(x)/D_(d-1)(x)].     (6)

If beta<=0, the bracket is decreasing in q, so its smallest value occurs at infinity. Nonnegativity there is equivalent, by (4) and the linear asymptotics, to H(infinity)=B-1/2>=0.

If beta>=0, the bracket is increasing in q. Thus middle-regime positivity for all s>=1 reduces solely to H(1)>=0. No restriction to s<=T is needed in either conclusion.

## 7. A complete all-dimensional branch and one remaining scalar test

For 0<=s<=1 let z=as and

    E(z)=[(1-z)^(1-d)-(1+z)^(1-d)]/[2z(d-1)].

Its power series E(z)=1+sum_(j>=1)c_j z^(2j) has strictly positive coefficients. In this regime

    H(s)=B-kappa E(z)+beta z E'(z).              (7)

If beta<=0, this is decreasing in s. Section 6 proves H(1)>=0 whenever B>=1/2, hence (3) holds at EVERY slope. Averaging under any centered law proves (2). In particular the all-dimensional upper dual is proved in the entire range kappa<=p, with no other new inequality.

For beta>=0 the positive series gives

    kappa E(z)-beta z E'(z)
      <=kappa+(kappa-2beta)_+[E(a)-1].            (8)

Indeed each nonconstant coefficient is kappa-2j beta<=kappa-2beta, and if the latter is negative all nonconstant coefficients are nonpositive. Therefore the explicit scalar condition

    B-kappa-(kappa-2beta)_+[E(a)-1]>=0            (9)

proves H>=0 in the small-s regime, including at s=1; Section 6 then proves H>=0 for every middle slope as well. This is a sufficient condition, not yet a proved inequality in the full parameter range.

There is a further exact endpoint reduction. Extend B affinely as B(kappa)=kappa e_*+1-v_*; this agrees with 1+t-kappa at the actual parameters. At kappa=p, identities (C) give

    B(p)=(1+t_*)/2>=1/2,  B(p)>=p.

Thus the already proved beta=0 certificate holds at kappa=p even if this lies below the actual interval. At kappa=kappa_1, (C) and the paid-fraction bound give B>=kappa. Affinity gives B>=kappa on the entire interval [p,kappa_1]. On that interval the left side of (9) is piecewise affine, with a single possible breakpoint at 2beta=kappa. At the breakpoint it equals B-kappa>=0, and at p it is the already proved H(1)>=0. Consequently it is enough to prove (9) only at kappa=kappa_1, whenever this endpoint has beta>0 and 2beta<kappa. This conclusion also covers the case kappa_0>p; it does not presume kappa_0<=p.

For clarity, the remaining single scalar test is therefore the following. Put

    F(R)=(dR-d+1)R^(-d)=(1-da)/(1-a)^d,
    p=(1-a)^d,  t_* = p/R^d,
    e_*=[(1-a)^(1-d)-R^(1-d)]/[2(d-1)(R-1)],
    v_*=(R-1+a)/[2(R-1)],
    K=(v_*+t_*)/(1+e_*),
    Z=a R^(d+1)(K/p-1)/[d(R-1)^2],
    E=[(1-a)^(1-d)-(1+a)^(1-d)]/[2a(d-1)].

For 0<a<1/d and the unique R>1+a, prove, in the only nontrivial branch 0<2Z<K,

    1+t_*-2K >= (K-2Z)(E-1).                    (10)

All denominators here are positive. The branches Z<=0 and 2Z>=K are already settled as above. The alternative parameter w=(1-a)/R in (0,1) removes the implicit root:

    1/(1-a)=d(1-w^(d-1))/[(d-1)(1-w^d)],
    R=(1-a)/w,  t_*=w^d.

Equation (10), rather than a claimed collapse of the full record hull, is the remaining sufficient upper-dual inequality.

The full centered record hull is therefore unnecessary. The actual remaining numerical task is an explicit upper-dual endpoint inequality, together with Rate's independent lower-dual obligation. No numerical observation is used as a proof of (9).
